source.title: SafeMERGE: Preserving Safety Alignment in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models via Selective Layer-Wise Model Merging
source.authors: Aladin Djuhera; S. Kadhe; Farhan Ahmed; Syed Zawad; Holger Boche

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites refusal-direction work as background, but its own method uses a weight-space, layer-wise safety subspace and merges LoRA updates; it does not test any listed version of the residual-stream direction claim.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates harmfulness after SafeMERGE, but this is a different intervention from finding, ablating, or adding the claimed residual-stream direction. The safety outcomes are recorded as findings about the related behavior, with versions set to none. It also reports general-ability and task-utility measures, which do not test the claimed direction or its ablation.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. (2024) only as background on shallow safety alignment and once when discussing general-ability retention. Its own method, SafeMERGE, uses a per-layer weight-space subspace (aligned minus base weights) to choose which LoRA layers to merge with a safety-tuned adapter. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless activation direction, never ablates or adds one, and never tests jailbreak mechanisms, transfer, or reasoning models. Its results are harmfulness rates of a mitigation method, which is outside the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SafeMERGE's selective layer-wise merging restores safety after fine-tuning while keeping task utility. They report it gives the best safety-utility trade-off among the evaluated post-fine-tuning and data-mixing baselines.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a per-layer weight-space subspace derived from aligned and unaligned model weights to decide which LoRA layers to merge with a safety-tuned model. It does not use a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream activation difference, or ablate/add that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on the similarity threshold and merging weights; higher thresholds merge more layers, improving safety at some cost to utility. The paper reports representative threshold optima of 0.7 for Llama-2, 0.75 for Llama-3.1, and 0.65 for Qwen-2 across tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign LoRA fine-tuning raises harmfulness on DirectHarm/HexPhi (e.g. Llama-2 GSM8K DirectHarm 5.0% to 27.8%). Selectively merging the layers that deviate from a weight-space safety subspace restores safety with little utility loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety degradation from fine-tuning concentrates in LoRA layers whose updates leave the aligned-minus-base weight subspace; merging those layers with a safety adapter restores safety. This is not evidence about the residual-stream refusal direction.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Safety is assessed with classifier-based harmfulness scores; the authors note this limitation. The main experiments tune hyperparameters on benchmark test sets, though they report a held-out split validation for Llama-3.1 on GSM8K. No uncertainty estimates are reported in the main results table.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the paper’s other defenses, utility metrics, or additional telecom-task safety outcomes: these evaluate SafeMERGE or other methods rather than the claimed direction. The paper’s cross-evaluator results are not separately extracted here.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means activation direction is computed, ablated or added.
No abliteration-style weight edit is made.
Jailbreaks are explicitly out of scope; no adversarial training against direction ablation.
No comparison of one direction against several.
No separation of harm judgment from refusal.
No transfer test. The weight-space subspace uses base and instruct weights but not the activation direction.
Benign fine-tuning degrades safety, but whether a removable direction exists is never examined.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': Arditi et al. is cited only in the introduction and in one aside on general-ability retention. The paper's 'safety direction' is a weight-space difference between instruct and base models (from SafeLoRA), not the activation difference-in-means direction. No verdict labels apply.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless activation difference direction is found or ablated/added across residual-stream layers and positions.
No weight edit implementing ablation of the claimed direction is tested.
No attack is tested for suppressing the claimed direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
No separation of harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions is tested.
No transfer of the claimed direction across languages, model variants, or base/instruct stages is tested.
The paper evaluates fine-tuning and safety restoration, but does not test whether training determines the existence of a removable direction.
No reasoning-model direction or refusal behavior is tested.
